cur:objects2-seal-simeon-i-bulgaria.summary: This lead seal of Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria carries on one face a frontal bust of Christ Pantokrator, his head set against a cross-nimbus and framed by a circular inscription, and on the other a bust of the Theotokos. Pressed onto the cords that closed a document, it placed the ruler's correspondence under the protection of Christ and his Mother. It shows how quickly the Byzantine image of Christ became part of the visual language of power among the newly Christian Slavs.
facts: The Commons record identifies the type as Iordanov Type III.2.A, the reference classification of Bulgarian medieval seals by Ivan Iordanov.
Simeon I (reigned 893–927), educated in Constantinople, presided over a flowering of Old Church Slavonic letters and claimed the imperial title of tsar.
Like Byzantine imperial seals, Bulgarian royal seals were struck in lead with a bulloterion (a pincer-like matrix) on cords attached to documents.
cur:objects2-seal-simeon-i-bulgaria.notes: The photographed specimen is a numismatic-trade piece (CNG); its present owner is not recorded. One entry stands for the seal type.

vam:O125665.summary: Within a small oval of dark green bloodstone, flecked with red, Christ appears in bust as the Pantocrator, the Ruler of All: frontal and austere, blessing with his right hand and holding a book in his left, with a cross-nimbus around his head and the letters IC XC at either side. The stone is now set in a later gold frame hung from a silver hook. Cameos like this were carried as amulets, appeals to Christ for help and protection.
facts: The V&A suggests that bloodstone may have been chosen deliberately: its natural red veins could recall Christ's sacrifice, making the stone part of the image's message.

Such hardstones could only be worked with rotating tools and abrasive grit; semi-precious materials were thought to reinforce the power of the images they carried, an attitude recorded by Michael Psellos (V&A).
Purchased in 1978 with the help of the Associates of the V&A; it was published by Paul Williamson in the Burlington Magazine in 1980.
vam:O125665.notes: Byzantine (Constantinople), ca. 10th century (V&A). Purchased from Rosewood Investments Ltd with the assistance of Michael van Rijn.
